claims.text: High-strain-rate loading produces a higher density of deformation twins than quasi-static loading.
The deformation twins generated during high-strain-rate loading are nanoscale.
Rapid dislocation accumulation at high strain rates triggers deformation-twin nucleation.
Twin-mediated obstruction of dislocation motion increases yield strength.
Deformation twins provide additional sites for slip and accommodate plastic deformation.
Dynamic loading at approximately 10^3 s^-1 will increase yield strength by more than about 10% relative to quasi-static loading at approximately 10^-3 s^-1.
Dynamic loading will enhance the strain-hardening rate relative to quasi-static loading.
Dynamic loading will enhance ductility relative to quasi-static loading.
TEM or EBSD will reveal significantly higher post-deformation twin density after dynamic loading than after quasi-static loading.
Under quasi-static loading, the baseline HEA deforms primarily by dislocation-mediated plasticity with minimal deformation twinning.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply to single-phase HEAs with moderate-to-low stacking-fault energy that permits twinning.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply at room temperature over strain rates high enough to activate twinning but below those causing substantial thermal effects or phase instability.
The proposed initial material has a single-phase, uniform microstructure and a grain size below 20 micrometers.
Such a single-phase, uniform, sub-20-micrometer microstructure is typically produced by casting or rapid solidification.
The magnitude of strength, ductility, and twin-density changes depends on alloy composition, initial grain size, and stacking-fault energy.
